4.5 off.text: A prime p > 3 is odd and coprime to 3, so p ≡ ±1 (mod 3) gives p² ≡ 1 (mod 3), and since any odd integer squared has the form (2k+1)² = 4k(k+1)+1 where k(k+1) is even, we get p² ≡ 1 (mod 8). By the Chinese Remainder Theorem, because gcd(3,8) = 1 and p² is congruent to 1 modulo both 3 and 8, it follows that p² ≡ 1 (mod 24). Therefore, for every prime p > 3, we have p² mod 24 = 1.

4.6 off.text: Since any prime p > 3 is odd and coprime to 3, we have p ≡ ±1 (mod 2) so p² ≡ 1 (mod 8), and p ≡ ±1 (mod 3) so p² ≡ 1 (mod 3). Because gcd(8, 3) = 1 and 8 · 3 = 24, the Chinese Remainder Theorem guarantees that p² ≡ 1 (mod 8) and p² ≡ 1 (mod 3) jointly yield p² ≡ 1 (mod 24). Therefore p² mod 24 = 1 for every prime p > 3.

4.7 off.text: Since p > 3 is prime, p is odd and not divisible by 3, so writing p = 2k+1 gives p² = 4k(k+1)+1 ≡ 1 (mod 8) because k(k+1) is always even, while p ≡ ±1 (mod 3) forces p² ≡ 1 (mod 3). By the Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT), since gcd(8,3) = 1 and 8·3 = 24, the pair of congruences p² ≡ 1 (mod 8) and p² ≡ 1 (mod 3) is equivalent to the single congruence p² ≡ 1 (mod 24). Therefore p² mod 24 = 1 for every prime p > 3.

AW susp.text: Since p > 3 is prime, p is coprime to both 8 and 3, so p is odd (giving p² ≡ 1 mod 8, because any odd integer is ±1 or ±3 mod 8 and each squares to 1) and p ≢ 0 mod 3 (giving p² ≡ 1 mod 3, since (±1)² = 1). By the Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT), the simultaneous congruences p² ≡ 1 mod 8 and p² ≡ 1 mod 3 lift uniquely to a single congruence modulo 24, namely p² ≡ 1 mod 24. Therefore every prime p > 3 satisfies p² mod 24 = 1.
